summary: ADR-0036 is sound and its measurable claims verify against the tree: SegmentCommit.segmentKey is a String checked only for non-emptiness (SegmentCommit.java:27-31), SegmentKey exposes only headerLenOf and no pod parser, golden/chain-delta-batched-v1.bin holds bins/a.seg and bins/b.seg with no pod byte in either, CheckpointWriter.java:129 merges on request.podId(), Checkpoint.java:151 is a strict version equality, CheckpointCursor.java:67 reports that IOException as store-unreachable, ChainReplay.java:371 LISTs from the seeded checkpoint and GETs every entry past it, ChainReplay.java:50 carries the never-GET-below javadoc, CheckpointTest.java:158-169 brackets ~38 KiB under 64 KiB at 1,600 streams, DefaultIngest.java:350 increments flushSeq unconditionally and discards published on failure, SegmentPublisher.java:136-141 PUTs on the unique-without-coordination premise, and the M3.0 golden quotation is verbatim. The cost lens is clean: no request rate here scales with records, shards, partitions or indices. Detection is an in-memory comparison against state recovered once per takeover; the answer path is one GET of a pointer the checkpoint already carries, bounded by replays; the checkpoint grows by fixed-width fields per pod, not with history; recovery reads nothing ChainReplay was not already going to read. One major remains, about what the accepted ADR leaves standing outside the diff.

findings.title: The ADR lands accepted while five production/testFixture javadoc sites still say the key is the bare pair, and the paragraph that required this to be handled is deleted in the same commit
findings.detail: The M4.10c note enumerates the superseded prose it found -- 'THE THREE DESCRIPTIVE SPEC.md SITES ARE THIS ROW'S: :55, :501 and :511' -- and all three verify. The sweep stopped at markdown. `git grep -n 'podId, flushSeq' -- '*.java'` returns five further sites in production and testFixtures, and unlike the SPEC.md three these are not merely incomplete, they are falsified by the ADR this commit accepts: CommitRequest.java:19 'is the idempotency key M4.10 will use to ignore a replay'; Sequencer.java:35-37 'NOT that a given (podId, flushSeq) is applied at most once -- that is M4.10 and does not hold yet', which after ADR-0036 will never hold, because a restarted pod legitimately reissues (podId, 0); Sequencer.java:51-53 'The pair is carried from this first commit precisely so M4.10 can make the retry safe without changing the record shape', while the ADR at :106 and backlog.md:123 require CommitRequest to GAIN incarnationId; FakeSequencer.java:27-29 'idempotency on (podId, flushSeq), which is M4.10's task and lands here in the same commit as the real behaviour so the two cannot drift'; Checkpoint.java:31-33, which cites that same M4.1 precedent to justify carrying a field early. No row in backlog.md or backlog-notes.md names any of them. What makes this a defect of THIS diff rather than a pre-existing one is that the same hunk deletes the instruction that forbade the state: the old M4.10c section read 'THE FORMAT ADR TRAVELS IN THIS COMMIT, not in M4.10b ... If M4.10b's decision pins BYTES rather than a key, then b and c are one commit and this row is absorbed -- say so in the ADR rather than leaving the tree between them contradicting an accepted decision.' The ADR's 'Which formats change' section does pin shape and placement, the row was not absorbed, and the ADR says nothing about the interim (grep for M4.10c in the ADR returns one line, ':89 This is the shape M4.10c was decomposed for'). The guardrail was removed and the state it guarded against was produced, in one commit, with no sentence saying why.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks up M4.10d (THE DEDUP). Its brief points it at CheckpointWriter's merge comment, so it opens the seam and reads Sequencer.java:46-53 -- the interface contract, the document a caller is told to read -- which says a retry becomes safe once the sequencer ignores a replay of a (podId, flushSeq) it has already applied, and FakeSequencer.java:27-29, which says the fake's idempotency lands in the same commit 'so the two cannot drift'. It implements dedup keyed on the pair in both. Every M4 test is single-incarnation: IngestCommitPathTest drives one DefaultIngest, BatchingSequencerTest supplies flushSeq literally (from("pod0", 0)), and no fixture restarts a pod. The suite is green, check-test-integrity sees no weakened assertion, and the shipped sequencer suppresses a restarted pod's reissued flushSeq 0 -- real commits dropped, the primary harm ADR-0036 opens by naming, re-entering through the one document the ADR did not touch. Separately, anyone budgeting M5's forwarding from Sequencer.java:51-53 will plan for no record-shape change when ADR-0036 has already decided there is one.
findings.remedy: Either name the five Java sites in the M4.10c and M4.10d notes the way :55/:501/:511 are named at backlog-notes.md:281, assigning each to the row whose blast radius already covers it, or add one sentence to ADR-0036 saying that the tree between M4.10b and M4.10c carries a superseded contract at those sites and which row retires it. Both are prose-sized and neither requires merging b and c.

findings.title: The reason attached to the fixture prescription is false for the first fixture it names; the prescription itself is right
findings.detail: ADR:118-121 and backlog-notes.md:261-263 say the three fixtures 'DIFFERENTIATE THEIR SEGMENTS ONLY BY POD TODAY, so they must be given differing incarnationId or flushSeq per segment -- differing pods alone leaves every encoded triple distinct only in a field a once-per-delta encoder can still hoist.' Measured against the first fixture named: BatchedCommitDeltaTest.java:41-45 builds a three-segment delta whose segments carry pod-a, pod-b and pod-c, and line 54 asserts `assertThat(decoded).isEqualTo(original)` -- whole-record equality, not a field probe. Once SegmentCommit carries podId, an encoder that writes one triple per delta cannot hoist three distinct podIds past that assertion; it decodes three segments all attributed to pod-a and the equality fails. podId is not hoistable when it varies and the decoded record is compared whole. The claim IS true of the other named fixture: BatchingSequencerTest.java:259-263 commits two pods and asserts only `delta.segments()).hasSize(2)` and a PUT count, which survives any placement; and the golden is written from whatever the implementation emits, so it guards later drift rather than the initial choice. The prescription is sound and strictly stronger than needed -- it also kills the partial hoist, where podId sits per segment and incarnationId/flushSeq sit once per delta, which is the shape none of the three fixtures would catch. Only the mechanism as worded is wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: A session building M4.10c checks the stated reason against the fixture the sentence names first, finds that three differing pods already kill a once-per-delta encoder under BatchedCommitDeltaTest.java:54, concludes the note is wrong, and drops the prescription -- losing it for BatchingSequencerTest, which asserts only segment COUNT and would let the partial hoist of incarnationId and flushSeq round-trip green all the way to M5's first forwarded multi-pod batch.

findings.title: A guard installed by a previous round's finding was deleted with the paragraph around it and is carried by nothing
findings.detail: The rewritten M4.10c section replaces 'Checkpoint is not a ChainEntry at all -- own MAGIC, own VERSION, no kind byte -- and ADR-0033 requires it never decode as one' with the two-line 'BOTH DELTA ENCODINGS CHANGE -- VERSION_DELTA for a single segment and the kinded batch.' The deleted sentence was not incidental prose: baselines/review.txt:28, unchanged in this commit, records why it exists -- 'ROUND 2 WAS A DEFECT I CREATED BY MERGING TWO FIXES INTO ONE SENTENCE: BOTH formats change ... as a new KIND, not a version bump is true only of the chain -- Checkpoint is not a ChainEntry ... so the row forbade the version bump it needs and prescribed a kind byte that does not exist. The two mechanisms are now stated separately, on purpose.' ADR-0036 does not pick it up: its Checkpoint bullet at :90-97 says only that decode must be made version-tolerant, and its 'Both delta encodings change' line at :127 is scoped to deltas. The retained 'OLD OBJECTS MUST STILL DECODE' paragraph anchors the version-tolerance half but says nothing about the kind byte or about ChainEntry.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10c reads 'BOTH DELTA ENCODINGS CHANGE ... both paths, or neither' beside a Checkpoint bullet that mentions only version tolerance, generalises the kind-byte mechanism across both formats as round 2 already did once, and either prescribes a KIND_* value for Checkpoint -- which has its own MAGIC and no kind field (Checkpoint.java:49, :112) and which ADR-0033 requires never decode as a ChainEntry -- or forbids the Checkpoint.VERSION bump the shape change needs. The exact defect the deleted sentence was written to prevent, with the record of why it was written sitting one file away in the same commit.

observations: M4/SPEC.md criterion 6 is NARROWED by this commit, from 'returns the original assignment' to 'returns the original assignment when the recorded pointer names a delta carrying that triple, refusing otherwise'. That is an acceptance criterion moving in the weakening direction. It is not raised as a finding because it is disclosed in place with an AMENDED banner naming ADR-0036, it is forced (answering an arbitrary earlier flushSeq needs either a pointer per flush, which grows with history against ADR-0033, or a backward chain walk, which is the unbounded read M4.9 removed), and the T0 mutation column at SPEC.md:469 was strengthened in the same hunk. It belongs in the commit body.

ADR-0036:73-79 admits the slot is destructible by an interleaving incarnation and defers the bound to M4.10d. That trades 'suppress real commits' for 'accept a duplicate under a same-podId interleave', which ADR-0031 declares out of protocol. Disclosed twice and assigned; not a finding.

ADR-0036:158-160 'No commit-path request scales with pods' is true of the normal path and of detection, and slightly overbroad for the replay branch, which issues one GET per detected replay. Since replays are exceptional and one pointer GET is O(1), no cost rule is breached; noted only so the sentence is not later quoted as covering the answer path.
